meaning: Puts the volitional form and 「まい」 of the same verb side by side to show you can't decide whether to do something or not.
connection: Verb volitional form + か + same verb dictionary form (or masu-stem) + まいか

senses.label: To do or not to do
senses.meaning: You can't make up your mind and keep going back and forth: “whether to go or not”, “whether to tell or not”. Often followed by 「迷う」, 「悩む」, or 「考える」.
senses.connection: Godan: 行こうか行くまいか; ichidan: 食べようか食べまいか; する: しようかするまいか／しようかしまいか
examples: I've been torn about whether to tell the truth or not.
I still haven't decided whether to go to the party.
I agonized for days over whether to study abroad.

notes: The volitional form and 「まい」 must come from the same verb: ✕「行こうか行かまいか」 ✕「行こうか帰るまいか」 → ○「行こうか行くまいか」.

Attaching 「まい」 is where learners slip. Godan verbs take the dictionary form (「言うまい」, not ✕「言わまい」); ichidan verbs take either the stem or the dictionary form (「食べまい／食べるまい」); 「する」 becomes 「するまい／すまい」 and 「来る」 becomes 「来るまい／こまい」.
It only expresses your own hesitation (or a character's in a novel). You can't use it to ask or tell someone else to decide: ✕「行こうか行くまいか、決めてください」 → ○「行くかどうか、決めてください」.
The tone is literary and a little stiff, so it can sound affected in casual chat. In conversation people say 「行こうかどうしようか迷ってる」 or 「行くかどうか迷ってる」.

daily.title: Should I confess?
daily.description: Telling a friend how torn you feel.
daily.example: I've been agonizing for a whole week over whether to confess my feelings.

daily.title: Can't decide on a purchase
daily.description: Hesitating in a shop over an expensive piece of clothing.
daily.example: I stood in front of the shop for thirty minutes, wondering whether to buy it or not.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's inner struggle.
daily.example: She stared at the phone, unsure whether to make the call or not.

work.title: Thinking about changing jobs
work.description: Talking with a senior colleague about whether to switch jobs.
work.example: I'm trying to decide whether to change jobs or not.

etymology: 「(よ)う」 is an auxiliary of intention, and 「まい」 is an old auxiliary of negative intention. Each takes the question marker 「か」. Placing “I will” and “I won't” side by side expresses being caught in a dilemma.

similar.title: 〜かどうか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜かどうか」 is a neutral “whether or not” and also works for other people and things (「明日晴れるかどうか分からない」). 「〜(よ)うか〜まいか」 is limited to acts of will you can decide yourself and stresses inner wavering. In speech, 「行くかどうか迷う」 is more common.

similar.title: 〜まい
similar.explanation: Same origin. The 「まい」 here is the negative-intention 「まい」, which on its own means a firm resolve not to do something (「もう二度と行くまい」 = “I'll never go again”). Only when paired with the volitional form does it turn into “to do or not to do”.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うが〜まいが／〜(よ)うと〜まいと
similar.explanation: Same origin. It is built the same way, with the volitional form and 「まい」 side by side, but is followed by 「が／と」 and means “whether you do it or not (it makes no difference)”: 「行こうが行くまいが、私の自由だ」. With 「か」 you are undecided; with 「が」 you don't care. One particle changes the meaning completely.

formation: This pattern is built from two self-questions placed side by side: the verb's volitional form + 「か」 (“Shall I do it?”) and the same verb + 「まい」 + 「か」 (“Shall I not?”). The volitional 「(よ)う」 means “intend to do”, and 「まい」 is its negative, “intend not to do”. Adding the question particle 「か」 to each gives one “yes” question and one “no” question. Setting the two opposite questions together captures the feeling of swinging back and forth, which is why 「迷う」, 「悩む」 and 「ためらう」 usually follow. Because it expresses hesitation of will, the action has to be something the speaker can decide. If you replace 「か」 with the concessive 「が」, you get 〜(よ)うが〜まいが, “whether you do it or not”.

meaning: Treats, sets, or defines A as B. Often used to state a purpose, target, standard, or focus.
connection: Noun A + を + Noun B + とする／として／とした (+ noun)

senses.label: Set A as B
senses.meaning: Sets A as B, typically a purpose, target, goal, or condition. Common in writing and formal settings. Similar to “with A as B” or “taking A as B”.
senses.connection: Aを目的／対象／目標／条件 + とする／として
examples: This survey targets high school students.
I study Japanese every day with the aim of studying abroad.

senses.label: Regard A as B
senses.meaning: Regards or treats A as B, or gives A a certain role: “treat A as B”.
senses.connection: Aを + リーダー／趣味／先生 etc. + として
examples: She looks up to Professor Yamada as her mentor.
The team chose him as their leader.

senses.label: Centered on A
senses.meaning: When modifying a noun, as in 「Aを中心とした」 or 「Aをテーマとした」, use 「とした／とする」. It means “centered on / themed on / based on A”.
senses.connection: Aを中心／テーマ／基準 + とした／とする + noun
examples: Heavy rain fell in areas centered on Tokyo.
A film about environmental issues is getting a lot of attention.

notes: The order of A and B can't be reversed. In 「AをBとする」 (“set A as B”), A is the thing being designated and B is the purpose, target, role, etc. ✕「目的を留学として」 → ○「留学を目的として」. Swapped, it makes no sense.
To modify a noun, use 「とした」 or 「とする」, not 「として」: ✕「若者を対象として商品」 → ○「若者を対象とした商品」.
Don't confuse it with the similar-looking 「〜(よ)うとする」 (“be about to / try to”). In 「書こうとする」 a verb's volitional form comes before 「とする」; here a noun + 「を」 and a noun B come before it.
「とする」 is more formal than 「にする」. Regulations, papers and notices write 「〜を目的とする」, while everyday speech says 「〜を目的にする」 or 「〜を中心にする」; using 「とする」 in conversation sounds stiff.

daily.title: Who a class is for
daily.description: Introducing a course at the community center.
daily.example: This class is for beginners.

daily.title: On the news
daily.description: A weather forecast describes the affected area.
daily.example: Rain is expected over a wide area centered on Kyushu.

work.title: Writing a proposal
work.description: Describing a product's target market in a proposal.
work.example: This product targets women in their twenties.

work.title: Company rules
work.description: An official document states the purpose of a policy.
work.example: The purpose of this program is to manage employees' health.

etymology: Made from the object marker 「を」, 「と」 marking content or result, and the verb 「する」. 「AをBとする」 originally meant “make A into B”, which extended to “set or regard A as B”.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: Same origin. A plain 「Bとして」 states the subject's own status or role (「留学生として来日した」). 「AをBとして」 designates a different thing, A, as B, so the object marker 「を」 is required: 「彼をリーダーとして選んだ」.

similar.title: 〜を中心に
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「Aを中心に」 is one of the set phrases of this pattern, also said 「Aを中心として／Aを中心とした」, and means “centered on A”. In this pattern B can also be 「目的」, 「対象」, 「テーマ」 and many other nouns.

similar.title: 〜を前提として
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and built the same way. 「Aを前提として」 means “taking A as a premise” (「結婚を前提として付き合う」) and is common in contracts and negotiations. The 「〜をBとする」 pattern covers a much wider range.

formation: It is formed from the object particle 「を」 + noun B + 「とする」. The 「と」 marks what something is taken to be, and 「する」 means “make, set”, so 「Bとする」 together means “set as B, treat as B”. Putting 「Aを」 in front names the thing being designated, giving “set A as B”. If B is 「目的」, 「対象」, 「中心」 or 「テーマ」, the sentence means A is the purpose, target, focus or theme. 「として」 is the te-form, used to connect to what follows; 「とした／とする」 is the attributive form, used to modify a noun, which is why you say 「若者を対象とした商品」.

meaning: “Is nothing more than ...”. Stresses that something has little value or significance, with a dismissive or coolly matter-of-fact tone.

senses.label: Nothing but ...
senses.meaning: States firmly that something is only a thing of limited worth: “is nothing but”, “is merely”. It often implies “it's no big deal”.
senses.connection: Noun + でしかない／でしかありません／でしかなかった
examples: That's nothing but an excuse.
I'm just an ordinary office worker.
His success was nothing more than luck.

senses.label: In the end, just ...
senses.meaning: Stresses that whatever you say, it is still only that thing at heart, and nothing more. Often paired with 「結局」, 「所詮」, or 「あくまで」.
senses.connection: 結局／所詮／あくまで + noun + でしかない
examples: No matter how expensive it is, it's just a tool in the end.
This is only one example, after all.

notes: It carries a belittling tone, so judging the other person or their work this way is very rude. Telling a client 「それは個人の感想でしかありません」 sounds arrogant; applied to yourself it is modest (「私は一社員でしかありません」).

It is an affirmative judgment, “is nothing more than...”, not a negative sentence. 「偶然でしかない」 means “it's merely chance”, not “it isn't chance”. If you read 「ない」 as a plain negation, you reverse the meaning.
Don't confuse it with 「〜でしか〜ない」 (“only by...”). In 「電車でしか行けない」, 「で」 is the means and the negative belongs to another verb; in 「でしかない」, 「で」 is the copula and 「ない」 follows directly.
It only attaches to nouns, not directly to verbs or adjectives: ✕「失敗したでしかない」 → ○「失敗でしかない」 or 「失敗したにすぎない」.

daily.title: Cheering up a friend
daily.description: A friend is down after one failure, and you tell them not to worry.
daily.example: One failure is just a step along the way.

daily.title: Being modest
daily.description: Responding humbly to praise.
daily.example: I'm still just a beginner.

daily.title: Reading an op-ed
daily.description: A critic attacks a government policy.
daily.example: This policy is nothing more than a stopgap.

work.title: A reminder in a meeting
work.description: Pointing out the limits of a figure.
work.example: This number is only a forecast, after all.

etymology: Made from 「で」 (the te-form of the copula 「だ」), the limiting 「しか」, and the negative 「ない」. Literally: “is not anything other than ...”.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both are “nothing more than...”. 「にすぎない」 also takes verbs and adjectives (「噂を聞いたにすぎない」) and sounds more objective. 「でしかない」 takes only nouns and is colder, with a stronger note of contempt or resignation.

similar.title: 〜しか〜ない
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「でしかない」 simply puts the copula 「で」 into the 「しか〜ない」 frame. Ordinary 「しか〜ない」 limits quantity or range (「千円しかない」 = “I only have 1,000 yen”); 「でしかない」 limits identity or nature.

similar.title: 〜にほかならない
similar.explanation: Often compared with it. 「にほかならない」 means “is none other than” and stresses a positive claim, typically naming the cause of success (「努力の結果にほかならない」). 「でしかない」 plays things down: “is merely”. Mix them up and the praise turns into put-down, or the reverse.

formation: It is formed from 「で」 (the continuative form of the copula 「だ」) + the limiting particle 「しか」 + the negative 「ない」. “Noun + である” originally identifies something as that noun; inserting 「しか〜ない」 turns it into “it is nothing but a noun”, working back to “only” from the negative side. That “this and nothing else” limit naturally implies “no greater value”, so the pattern is mostly used to belittle, play down or speak modestly. Since the core is “noun + である”, only a noun can come before it.

title: 〜以上に (exceeding)
meaning: Shows that something goes beyond a certain standard: “more than ...”, “even more than ...”.

senses.label: Beyond expectations
senses.meaning: Reality goes beyond what was expected or hoped. Common set phrases: 「予想以上に」, 「思った以上に」, 「想像以上に」, 「期待以上に」.
senses.connection: 予想／想像／期待 + 以上に; verb ta-form + 以上に
examples: The exam was harder than I expected.
This job takes more time than I thought.

senses.label: Even more than ...
senses.meaning: The degree is higher compared with something else: “even more ... than”. Common: 「前回以上に」, 「去年以上に」, 「誰以上に」.
senses.connection: Noun + 以上に + adjective／verb
examples: He is even taller than his older brother.
I hear this year will be even hotter than last year.

senses.label: Even more (emphasis)
senses.meaning: With 「それ以上に」 or 「これまで以上に」, it means something else matters even more, or something is stronger than ever before.
senses.connection: それ／これまで／今まで + 以上に
examples: Money is important, but health is even more important.
I will work harder than ever.

notes: Don't confuse it with 「〜以上(は)」 (“now that...”). 「約束した以上に頑張る」 means “try harder than promised”, while 「約束した以上は守る」 means “since I promised, I'll keep it”. One particle, 「に」 versus 「は」, changes the meaning completely.
After a number, 「以上」 means “or more” and includes that number: 「二十歳以上」 includes twenty-year-olds. This has nothing to do with the “exceeds a degree” meaning here.
Use 「以上の」 before a noun and 「以上に」 before a verb or adjective: ✕「予想以上に結果」 → ○「予想以上の結果」.
「これ以上〜ない」 and 「それ以上〜ない」 mean “no more...” (「これ以上待てない」 = “I can't wait any longer”), not “more... than this”.

daily.title: After a trip
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about a trip.
daily.example: Kyoto was an even more beautiful city than I had imagined.

daily.title: Reviewing a restaurant
daily.description: Your verdict after a meal.
daily.example: The ramen at this shop is even better than people say.

work.title: Reporting sales
work.description: Telling your boss how a new product is selling.
work.example: The new product is selling better than expected.

work.title: New Year speech
work.description: The company president encourages employees at the start of the year.
work.example: This year will probably be even tougher than last year.

etymology: 「以上」 originally means “above this point”. With the adverbial 「に」, it shows that a degree goes beyond some standard.

similar.title: 〜にもまして
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both are “even more than...”. 「にもまして」 is more literary and stresses that the earlier item was already high and the later one is higher still (「以前にもまして忙しい」); it also gives 「何にもまして」 (“more than anything”). 「以上に」 is more common and often pairs with 「予想」 and 「思った」.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「AよりBのほうが」 compares two things neutrally. 「A以上に」 stresses that the baseline A was exceeded, especially expectations or previous years, with more exclamatory force: 「予想以上に難しかった」 emphasizes surprise more than 「予想より難しかった」.

similar.title: 〜以上(は)
similar.explanation: Same origin (the same 「以上」). 「〜以上(は)」 follows a plain-form verb and gives a condition, “since...” (「引き受けた以上は最後までやる」). This pattern expresses exceeding a degree; the telltale difference is whether 「は」 or 「に」 follows.

formation: 「以上」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “above this point”. Put a baseline for comparison before it (「予想」, 「去年」, 「思った」) and 「〜以上」 means “a degree beyond that baseline”. Adding the adverbial 「に」 lets it modify the verb or adjective that follows: “to a degree beyond the baseline”, that is, “more than...”. Because the baseline is what you compare against, the most common uses are 「予想以上に」 and 「思った以上に」, “the reality exceeded expectations”. Swap 「に」 for 「の」 and it modifies a noun, as in 「予想以上の人出」.

meaning: “Doing ... doesn't mean ...”, “that doesn't count as ...”. Rejects a conclusion or judgment someone might draw.
connection: Verb plain form (usually ta-form) + ことにはならない

senses.label: Doesn't mean ...
senses.meaning: A certain fact doesn't lead to a certain conclusion: “that doesn't mean ...”. Often paired with 「〜からといって」 or 「〜だけで」.
senses.connection: 〜からといって + verb plain form + ことにはならない
examples: Reading something once doesn't mean you've understood it.
Staying silent doesn't mean you agree.

senses.label: Doesn't count as ...
senses.meaning: An action falls short, so it can't be counted as having done something: “that doesn't count as ...”. The 「は」 can be dropped: 「ことにならない」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ことには(／に)ならない
examples: Just apologizing doesn't mean you've taken responsibility.
Just copying the textbook doesn't count as studying.

notes: Don't use it for feelings or attitudes; use 「わけではない」 instead: ✕「嫌いなことにはならない」 → ○「嫌いなわけではない」 (“it's not that I dislike it”). This pattern judges whether an action counts as something.
The first part is usually a specific completed action (often in the ta-form), and 「〜だけでは」 or 「〜からといって」 often points out why it falls short: 「一度読んだだけでは、理解したことにはならない」.
The 「こと」 in 「大変なことにならないように」 is a real “thing” and this is the negative of 「ことになる」 (“turn out that...”), not the pattern here.
Telling a superior or client 「それでは謝ったことにはなりません」 amounts to lecturing them and is very blunt. When you need to point it out, say something softer such as 「もう少しご説明いただけると助かります」.

daily.title: Don't jump to conclusions
daily.description: A friend thinks they're disliked because the other person hasn't replied.
daily.example: Just because they haven't replied doesn't mean they dislike you.

daily.title: A parent teaching a child
daily.description: The child says they've finished copying their homework.
daily.example: Just copying the answers doesn't count as doing your homework.

work.title: A reminder in a meeting
work.description: Telling colleagues not to judge by surface figures.
work.example: Sales going up doesn't mean the problem is solved.

work.title: Reading an op-ed
work.description: An expert comments on how well a policy works.
work.example: Just passing a law doesn't mean discrimination has disappeared.

etymology: Made from the formal noun 「こと」, 「になる」 (result), and a negative. 「〜ことになる」 means “it amounts to ...”. Its negative, with the contrastive 「は」, means “it doesn't amount to ...”.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can be “it's not that...”. 「わけではない」 denies a conclusion that naturally follows from the situation, or the speaker's state (「嫌いなわけではない」). 「ことにはならない」 focuses on an action not counting as something (「読んだだけでは理解したことにはならない」).

similar.title: 〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「とは限らない」 means “not necessarily...” and leaves room for possibility (「高いものが良いとは限らない」). 「ことにはならない」 flatly rules it out, “doesn't count”, and is more decisive.

similar.title: 〜たことにする・〜たことになる
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜たことになる」 means “counts as, amounts to” (「これで半分終わったことになる」). This pattern is its negative plus 「は」, “can't be counted as”.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: Same origin. Besides “it follows that...”, 「ことになる」 means “it has been decided” (「来月転勤することになった」). The negative 「ことにならなかった」 in that sense means “it wasn't decided”, which differs from “doesn't count” here.

formation: It is formed from the formal noun 「こと」 + 「になる」 + the contrastive particle 「は」 + a negative. 「〜たことになる」 files an action under some evaluation, “counts as...”; negated, it means “can't be filed there, doesn't count”. The inserted 「は」 singles that evaluation out for denial, giving the nuance “whatever else may be true, it at least doesn't count as this”. Since the pattern judges whether something counts, a specific action that has already been done usually comes first, along with 「〜だけでは」 or 「〜からといって」 explaining what is lacking, giving “merely doing... doesn't amount to...”.

title: 〜ままに (following along)
meaning: Acting by going along with your feelings, what others say, or the natural flow of things: “as ... pleases”, “just as ... says”.
connection: Verb dictionary form／ta-form／passive form + ままに; noun + の + ままに

senses.label: As you please
senses.meaning: Doing something just as you feel, without holding back. Common: 「気の向くままに」, 「足の向くままに」, 「思いつくままに」, 「感じるままに」.
senses.connection: 気の向く／足の向く／思う／感じる + ままに
examples: On my days off, I wander around town wherever my mood takes me.
I wrote in my diary whatever came to mind.
I kept traveling wherever my feet led me.

senses.label: Just as you're told
senses.meaning: Doing exactly what others say or ask, with no will of your own. Often with the passive: 「言われるままに」, 「勧められるままに」.
senses.connection: Verb passive form + ままに
examples: I just went along with the clerk's suggestions and ended up buying expensive clothes.
He works doing whatever his boss tells him.

senses.label: Giving in to ...
senses.meaning: Noun + 「の」: following a desire, an order, or a natural state. Common: 「欲望のままに」, 「命令のままに」, 「心のままに」. Mostly written language.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ままに
examples: He lives giving in to his desires.
Just sing as your heart tells you.

notes: With the passive, 「言われるままに」 or 「勧められるままに」, it carries regret or self-mockery about yourself, and implies “no mind of their own, pushed around” about others. Saying 「言われるままにやっていますね」 to a superior or elder to their face is very rude.
Don't confuse it with 「〜たまま」, which means “remaining as is”: 「靴を履いたまま入る」 is “go in with your shoes on” (state unchanged), while 「言われるままに書く」 is “write whatever they tell me” (compliance).
After a noun add 「の」; verbs connect directly: ✕「欲望ままに」 → ○「欲望のままに」; ○「思いつくままに」.
「〜のままに」 can also mean “as it was”: 「昔のままに残っている」 is “remains just as it was”, not “at the mercy of”. Judge by the verb that follows.

daily.title: Talking about travel style
daily.description: Telling a friend how you like to travel.
daily.example: I like to travel without plans, going wherever I feel like.

daily.title: Regretting an impulse buy
daily.description: Complaining to family that a salesperson talked you into it.
daily.example: I signed the contract just because they told me to, and now I regret it.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's reckless life.
daily.example: The man lived by his desires and lost everything.

work.title: Advice from a senior
work.description: A senior tells a new employee to think for themselves.
work.example: If you only do what your boss tells you, you won't grow.

etymology: 「まま」 is written 「儘」 and originally means “as it is, as one likes”. With 「に」 it works as an adverb: “acting in line with ...”.

similar.title: 〜ままに (as one pleases / just as is)
similar.explanation: The closest entry. It also means “at the mercy of, following”, and covers “doing it just as is” (「見たままに話す」). This entry centers on “as one pleases” and “being pushed around”.

similar.title: 〜ままに・〜られるままに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning, specifically the passive 「〜られるままに」. It stresses giving in to others without resisting (「誘われるままに」), has a stronger negative tone, and is mostly written language.

similar.title: 〜とおりに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can be “as...”. 「とおりに」 means doing exactly as instructed or planned, neutral or even positive (「説明書のとおりに組み立てる」). 「ままに」 means going along with something, lacking your own judgment, and often sounds casual or passive.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「まま」 itself means “remaining in the same state” (「窓を開けたまま寝た」). With 「に」 before verbs of compliance, it extends to “doing as things are”.

formation: 「まま」 (儘) originally means “as it is, the original state”. Put 「気の向く」, 「言われる」 or 「欲望の」 before it and it means “as one's mood is”, “as one is told”, “as one's desire is”. With the adverbial 「に」 modifying the action that follows, the sense is “doing it just as that is, without altering anything”. Not altering anything, and not adding your own judgment, produces “going along with, following”. With your own feelings as the subject it is “as one pleases”; with the passive, following other people's words, it is “doing whatever you're told”, so it often carries a negative note of having no will of one's own.

meaning: Given the situation just described, it is only natural or understandable that something happens.
connection: Verb／adjective plain form (na-adjective + な) + のも当然だ／のももっともだ

senses.label: It's only natural that ...
senses.meaning: First give the reason, then say the result is natural: “it's no wonder ...”, “of course ...”. The tone is fairly objective and calm.
senses.connection: Plain form + のも当然だ／のも当然です／のも当然のことだ
examples: You practice every day, so of course you're getting better.
After working that hard, it's only natural to be tired.

senses.label: It's understandable that ...
senses.meaning: 「のももっともだ」 puts you in the other person's shoes and says their reaction or opinion is reasonable: “no wonder ...”, “you have a point”.
senses.connection: Plain form + のももっともだ／のももっともです
examples: If someone broke three promises to her, no wonder she's angry.
It's understandable that you'd think that way.

notes: Saying 「〜のも当然だ」 about someone else's failure or loss amounts to “serves you right”; to a superior, 「失敗されるのも当然です」 is extremely rude. To show you understand their feelings, use 「〜のも無理はありません」 or 「〜のももっともです」.
You must nominalize the clause with 「の」: ✕「怒るも当然だ」 → ○「怒るのも当然だ」. Nouns and na-adjectives need 「な」: 「心配なのも当然だ」.
Sentence-initial 「もっとも、〜」 means “though, that said” and is unrelated: 「もっとも、例外もある」.

daily.title: Understanding a friend's feelings
daily.description: A friend complains a coworker betrayed them, and you show you understand.
daily.example: If someone did that to you, no wonder you're angry.

daily.title: A popular restaurant
daily.description: Your reaction to a long line outside a restaurant.
daily.example: If it's this good, no wonder there's a line.

work.title: Analyzing a complaint
work.description: Discussing in a meeting why a client is unhappy.
work.example: The delivery was two weeks late, so it's only natural that the client is dissatisfied.

work.title: On the news
work.description: A commentator discusses public reaction to a policy.
work.example: If tax increases continue, it's understandable that the public will push back.

etymology: The nominalizer 「の」 turns the preceding clause into a noun. Then 「も」 (“also”) is added, followed by 「当然だ」 (natural) or 「もっともだ」 (reasonable) as the predicate.

similar.title: 〜のも無理はない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can be “no wonder...”. 「のも無理はない」 stresses sympathy and is mostly used for negative feelings and reactions (「怒るのも無理はない」). 「のも当然だ」 is more objective and calm, and works for good and bad results alike.

similar.title: 〜のももっともだ
similar.explanation: This separate entry for 「のももっともだ」 focuses on the other person's thinking or reaction being reasonable, often agreeing with their opinion (「あなたがそう言うのももっともだ」); see it for more examples.

similar.title: 〜て当然だ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (it also uses 「当然」). 「〜て当然だ」 attaches directly to the te-form and often carries an evaluation of “that's only as it should be”, even blame (「謝って当然だ」). 「のも当然だ」 stresses that the result naturally follows from the cause and sounds more objective.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「わけだ」 is the speaker drawing a conclusion from the facts, an “aha, so that's why” (「道理で安いわけだ」 = “no wonder it's cheap”). 「のも当然だ」 evaluates the result as only to be expected.

formation: The formal noun 「の」 turns the preceding clause (「彼が怒る」) into a “thing”. 「も」 means “this too”, implying “given the circumstances, even this result”. 「当然だ」 or 「もっともだ」 then serves as the predicate that judges it. The sentence is therefore typically “reason (「〜のだから／〜たら」) + result + 「のも当然だ」”, presenting the result as reasonable given its cause. 「当然」 is “only logical” and more objective; 「もっとも」 is “reasonable and understandable”, so 「のももっともだ」 is often used to show understanding of or agreement with someone's feelings and opinions.

meaning: From common sense or someone's position, something is just as it should be: “it's only natural that ...”.
connection: Verb te-form／i-adjective くて／na-adjective・noun で + 当然だ

senses.label: Only natural
senses.meaning: In a given situation, a certain result or reaction is completely natural: “it's only natural that ...”, “no wonder ...”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + 当然だ／当然です
examples: You worked so hard, so of course you passed.
It's your first time, so it's normal to make mistakes.

senses.label: As it should be
senses.meaning: From someone's position or duty, this is what they ought to do. It often sounds like “that's the least you should do”, sometimes as a criticism.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + 当然だ (negative: 〜なくて当然)
examples: It's only natural for parents to worry about their children.
If you're a professional, you should be able to do this much.

senses.label: Adjective + 当然
senses.meaning: After adjectives or nouns, 「くて当然」 or 「で当然」 says it's natural to have that quality.
senses.connection: i-adjective くて／na-adjective で + 当然だ
examples: It's close to the station, so of course the rent is high.
Kids are supposed to be lively.

notes: Used about others, it often carries a “that's what you're supposed to do” judgment, even blame. If someone helped you, 「手伝ってくれて当然だ」 means “you should help me”, which is extremely rude; telling a client 「ご確認いただいて当然です」 also offends.
The connection with adjectives and nouns is easy to get wrong: i-adjectives take 「くて当然」, and nouns and na-adjectives take 「で当然」. ✕「高い当然だ」 → ○「高くて当然だ」; ○「子供は元気で当然だ」.
The 「として」 in 「として当然だ」 means “as (a)”, not a te-form: 「医者として当然のことをしたまでです」.
To modify a noun, use 「〜て当然の」: 「言われて当然のことだ」.

daily.title: Calming a nervous friend
daily.description: A friend is nervous about their first time on stage.
daily.example: It's your first time on stage, so of course you're nervous.

daily.title: Lecturing a child
daily.description: A parent scolds a child for not greeting people.
daily.example: When you meet someone, you're supposed to say hello, right?

work.title: Praising a team member
work.description: A boss talks about a high-performing subordinate.
work.example: He prepared so thoroughly, so of course he won the contract.

work.title: Customer service attitude
work.description: A store manager stresses service in training.
work.example: Treating customers politely is the bare minimum.

etymology: The conjunctive particle 「て」 links to 「当然だ」. 「当然」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “as it should be”.

similar.title: 〜のも当然だ・〜のももっともだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「のも当然だ」 first nominalizes the clause, often pairs with 「〜のだから」, and sounds objective. 「て当然だ」 attaches straight to the te-form, is more colloquial, and carries more of a “that's how it ought to be” judgment.

similar.title: 〜てしかるべきだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜てしかるべきだ」 also means “it should be so”, but is more literary and formal, mostly used to argue that some treatment or handling is warranted (「謝罪があってしかるべきだ」).

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「べきだ」 directly asserts a duty or gives advice, “you should” (「謝るべきだ」). 「て当然だ」 judges that something is only natural, focusing on evaluating the result or action rather than commanding or advising.

formation: It is formed from the conjunctive particle 「て」 + the na-adjective 「当然だ」. 「て」 presents the preceding action or state (「合格する」, 「心配する」) as a whole, and 「当然だ」 passes judgment on it, literally “it's natural to have done...”. Since it evaluates the action itself, when that action is someone else's duty it brings out “as it should be”, even blame (「謝って当然だ」). Adjectives and nouns connect to 「当然だ」 through 「くて」 and 「で」 in the same way, meaning that having some quality is only natural.

meaning: Read 「なか」. Doing something in the middle of a (usually unfavorable) situation or environment, or under certain circumstances.
connection: Verb・i-adjective plain form／noun + の + 中を・中で・中では

senses.label: Braving ...
senses.meaning: Doing something despite bad weather or difficult conditions: “in the rain”, “braving the cold”. Usually followed by verbs of movement like 「来る」, 「歩く」, 「出かける」.
senses.connection: 雨／雪／寒い／暑い + 中を
examples: Many people came out for us despite the rain.
Thank you for coming all this way in the cold.

senses.label: Despite being busy
senses.meaning: A polite set phrase thanking or apologizing to someone who made an effort at an inconvenient time. 「お忙しい中」 and 「お足元の悪い中」 are fixed expressions.
senses.connection: お忙しい／お足元の悪い + 中(を)
examples: Thank you for coming despite your busy schedule.
Thank you very much for coming despite the bad weather.

senses.label: Amid ...
senses.meaning: Something happens while a certain situation continues: “amid ...”, “in a situation where ...”. Mostly in news and writing. Common: 「〜が続く中で」, 「〜する中で」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form・ている form + 中で／中では
examples: Even as the recession continues, some companies are growing their sales.
The match began as a large crowd looked on.

notes: The 「中」 here is read 「なか」: 「お忙しい中」 is 「おいそがしいなか」, never 「ちゅう」. Only words like 「会議中（かいぎちゅう）」 and 「一日中（いちにちじゅう）」 use the on-reading. Misreading it in a speech is embarrassing.

「お忙しい中」, 「お足元の悪い中」 and 「お寒い中」 are set courteous phrases for thanking or apologizing to the other person, showing consideration for them. You can't use them to stress your own hardship: 「忙しい中、来てやったんだ」 sounds like taking credit and is rude.
Nouns need 「の」; verbs and adjectives connect directly: ✕「雨中を」 → ○「雨の中を」; ○「寒い中」, 「雨が降る中」.
「部屋の中で本を読む」 is just the literal “inside the room” and not this pattern. Here 「中」 refers to weather, circumstances or conditions.

daily.title: Thanking a visiting friend
daily.description: A friend came to see you in the rain.
daily.example: I'm so happy you came all the way here in the rain.

daily.title: On the news
daily.description: A news report on a marathon.
daily.example: In strong winds, the runners ran all the way to the finish.

work.title: Opening a meeting
work.description: The host thanks the attendees.
work.example: Thank you all for taking time out of your busy schedules to be here today.

work.title: Annual report
work.description: Describing the business environment in a report.
work.example: Despite a tough market environment, the company secured a profit.

etymology: 「中(なか)」 originally means “inside”. It extended from being physically inside something to being in a kind of weather, situation, or circumstance.

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「最中に」 stresses “right in the middle of... (when something else suddenly happens)” (「会議の最中に電話が鳴った」). 「中を」 focuses on persevering in an unfavorable situation, or politely thanking the other person.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can mean “regardless of...”. 「もかまわず」 stresses not caring or minding (「人目もかまわず泣いた」) and often carries a negative judgment. 「雨の中を」 merely describes acting in an unfavorable environment, and in courteous phrases it also conveys thanks.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. Both 「お忙しいにもかかわらず」 and 「お忙しい中」 can be used to thank someone. 「にもかかわらず」 is the concessive “in spite of”, more formal and stiff; 「中」 is a softer courtesy phrase, more common in speeches.

similar.title: 〜中 (じゅう / ちゅう)
similar.explanation: Same origin (the same kanji 「中」). Read 「じゅう」 it means “throughout” (「一日中」); read 「ちゅう」 it means “in the middle of” (「会議中」). This pattern is read 「なか」 and means “within a situation”.

formation: 「中（なか）」 originally means “inside”. Put an element describing an environment or situation before it (「雨の」, 「寒い」, 「お忙しい」) and that situation is treated as a “space” the person is in. Adding 「を」, which marks the place passed through, gives “go through this space and act”, hence “come in spite of the rain or the cold”. Adding 「で（は）」 gives “within this situation”, extended to “under such circumstances”. The courtesy phrase 「お忙しい中」 pictures the other person's busyness as a hard-to-cross environment and thanks them for “passing through it” to be here.

meaning: Shows the direction, target, or goal of an action: “toward ...”, “facing ...”, “at ...”.
connection: Noun + に向かって／に向かい／に向かう

senses.label: Toward (direction)
senses.meaning: Movement or action heading in a direction or to a place: “toward ...”, “heading for ...”.
senses.connection: Place・direction noun + に向かって + verb of movement
examples: The ship is heading south.
I'm on my way to the station now.

senses.label: At / to (a person or thing)
senses.meaning: Doing something while facing someone or something, especially speaking or showing an attitude: “to ...”, “at ...”. 「親に向かって」 is often used to scold someone for talking back.
senses.connection: Person・thing + に向かって + 言う／叫ぶ／頭を下げる etc.
examples: How dare you talk to your parents like that!
He shouted at the sea at the top of his voice.

senses.label: Toward (a goal or trend)
senses.meaning: Working toward a goal, or a situation moving in some direction: “toward ...”, “on the way to ...”. Common: 「夢に向かって」, 「快方に向かう」, 「春に向かって」.
senses.connection: Goal・state noun + に向かって／に向かう
examples: I work hard every day toward my dream.
My father's illness is getting better.

notes: Followed by criticism, 「親に向かって」 or 「先生に向かって」 means “how dare you say that to...'s face”, a scolding phrase: 「親に向かってその口のきき方は何だ」. To say politely that you are addressing someone, use 「〜に」 or 「〜に対して」, not 「〜に向かって申し上げます」.
To mean “in preparation for...”, 「に向けて」 sounds more natural: ✕「来月の発売に向かって準備している」 → ○「来月の発売に向けて準備している」. 「に向かって」 focuses on direction and facing.
「向かう」 is intransitive, so its target takes 「に」 or 「へ」, not 「を」: ✕「海を向かって叫ぶ」 → ○「海に向かって叫ぶ」. (Only 「前を向く」, with 「向く」, takes 「を」.)
To modify a noun, use 「〜に向かう＋noun」 or 「〜に向かっての＋noun」: 「駅に向かう人々」.

daily.title: Saying where you are on the phone
daily.description: A friend calls and asks where you are.
daily.example: I've already left home and I'm heading your way.

daily.title: Graduation speech
daily.description: A teacher encourages graduates.
daily.example: Please keep working toward your own dreams.

daily.title: Weather forecast
daily.description: A forecaster describes a typhoon's path.
daily.example: The typhoon is moving north.

work.title: Project kickoff
work.description: A manager rallies the team.
work.example: Let's all work together toward reaching our goal.

work.title: Reporting performance
work.description: Explaining results to the board.
work.example: Our results are on the road to recovery.

etymology: The verb 「向かう」 (face, head for) in te-form, with the particle 「に」. 「向かう」 comes from 「向く」 (to face) and means “to head in a direction”.

similar.title: 〜に向けて
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「向く」). 「に向けて」 is the te-form of the transitive 「向ける」 and means “in preparation for...” or “aimed at a target” (「試験に向けて勉強する」, 「若者に向けて発信する」). 「に向かって」 focuses on direction and facing.

similar.title: 〜向け
similar.explanation: Same origin. After a noun, 「〜向け」 means “intended for...” (「子供向けの本」) and stresses the audience it was designed for. 「に向かって」 expresses the direction an action faces or the target it is aimed at.

similar.title: 〜へ (direction)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「へ」 only marks the direction of movement (「駅へ行く」). 「に向かって」 emphasizes the posture of facing toward something and can also mean speaking to someone or working toward a goal.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (both can be “toward”). 「に対して」 expresses the target of an action or attitude, abstract and formal (「質問に対して答える」). 「に向かって」 is more concrete and stresses facing someone head-on (「親に向かって文句を言う」).

formation: It is formed from the case particle 「に」 + the te-form of the verb 「向かう」. 「向かう」 derives from 「向く」 (face toward) and means “face or head toward a place”. 「に」 marks the destination or target, and the te-form 「向かって」 modifies the action that follows: “toward it, (do...)”. When the target is a place it means “move in a direction”; when it is a person it becomes “facing someone (speaking, shouting)”, with a sense of confronting them head-on, which is why 「親に向かって」 implies “daring to say it to a parent's face”. With an abstract goal or state it extends to “work toward a goal” or “things are heading toward...” (「快方に向かう」).

meaning: A formal, written version of the particle 「で」. Marks place, means, time, cause, and so on.

senses.label: Place
senses.meaning: Where something happens or is held. Same as 「で」. Common in notices, announcements, and invitations.
senses.connection: Place noun + にて
examples: The information session will be held on the third floor of the head office building.
Reception is in the first-floor lobby.

senses.label: Means / method
senses.meaning: Means, method, or medium. Same as 「で」. Common: 「メールにて」, 「書面にて」, 「電話にて」.
senses.connection: Means noun + にて
examples: We will let you know the results by email at a later date.
Please apply in writing.

senses.label: Time / deadline
senses.meaning: A point in time or a deadline. Same as 「で」. 「これにて」 is a set phrase meaning “with this, (we end)”.
senses.connection: Time noun／これ + にて
examples: This concludes today's meeting.
This sale ends at the end of this month.

senses.label: Cause / reason
senses.meaning: A cause or reason. Same as 「で」. Less common, mostly in formal notices.
senses.connection: Cause noun + にて
examples: Due to bad weather, today's event has been canceled.

notes: 「にて」 is only for written, formal contexts. In everyday speech, 「駅にて待ってる」 sounds like reading out an official notice, which is odd; use 「で」 in conversation.
It can only replace 「で」 marking place, means, time or reason, not the 「で」 meaning “is”: ✕「私は学生にて、〜」 → ○「私は学生で、〜」. It can't replace the 「で」 of totals such as 「三つで千円」 either.
「これにて」 is a set phrase meaning “with this (we close)”: 「これにて閉会いたします」. Don't read it as “using this”.
「メールにて失礼いたします」 in business email is a courtesy phrase meaning “forgive me for contacting you by email (not in person)”, and it is polite to clients and superiors, so you can use it as is.

daily.title: A shop notice
daily.description: A sign at a shop entrance about business hours.
daily.example: We will close at 6 p.m. today.

daily.title: A wedding invitation
daily.description: The invitation states the venue.
daily.example: The ceremony will be held at a hotel in the city.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Telling a client how you'll contact them.
work.example: We will send you the details in a separate email.

work.title: Closing a meeting
work.description: The chair announces the end of the meeting.
work.example: With that, I declare the meeting closed.

etymology: A combination of the classical particle 「に」 and the conjunctive particle 「て」, which marked place, means, and so on in classical Japanese. In speech it contracted to 「で」, while 「にて」 survived as a written form.

similar.title: 〜で (place of action)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「で」 is the everyday default (「会議室で行う」). 「にて」 means the same, but is used only in formal documents such as announcements, notices and invitations.

similar.title: 〜で (means, method)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. For means, 「メールで送る」 is the ordinary phrase and 「メールにてお送りします」 is more formal, common in business email and official notices.

similar.title: 〜において
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「において」 is also a written way to mark place or occasion, better suited to large events or abstract fields (「教育において」, 「東京において開催される」). 「にて」 is mostly for concrete places and means and can't express “in terms of...”.

similar.title: 〜をもって
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「をもって」 is also formal and can express means (「書面をもって通知する」) and a deadline (「本日をもって終了する」), with a more solemn tone than 「にて」.

formation: It combines the case particle 「に」 + the conjunctive particle 「て」. In classical Japanese 「に」 marks the place or state, and 「て」 links it to the following action, so 「にて」 means “in (that state), doing...”, extending to place, means, reason and so on. The modern case particle 「で」 is generally thought to have developed from 「にて」 by contraction in speech. So 「にて」 and 「で」 correspond almost one to one in meaning, but 「にて」, as the preserved older form, sounds formal and literary and appears only in notices, business documents and speeches.

meaning: “From the point of view of ...”, “on ...”. Often hints that the reality may be different.
connection: Noun + の上では／の上で(も); noun + 上(じょう)は

senses.label: On paper / according to ...
senses.meaning: Looking at things from one angle, such as data, documents, or rules. Often implies “that's how it looks, but the reality may differ”: “on paper”, “according to ...”.
senses.connection: 数字／書類／計算／暦／法律 etc. + の上では
examples: According to the numbers, the economy is recovering.
By the calendar it's already spring, but it's still cold.
On paper, there are no problems.

senses.label: In terms of ...
senses.meaning: In a certain area or respect. You can also say 「の上でも」: “in terms of ...”, “when it comes to ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + の上でも／の上で
examples: For your health, too, early to bed and early to rise is important.
He is very strict when it comes to work.

senses.label: 〜上(じょう)は
senses.meaning: A Sino-Japanese noun directly + 「上(じょう)」 is a shorter, written form with the same meaning, as in 「法律上」, 「形式上」, 「計算上」.
senses.connection: Sino-Japanese noun + 上(じょう)は／上では／上の
examples: Legally there's no problem, but morally there are still questions.
By our calculations, there should be plenty of profit.

notes: 「の上では」 often hints that “in reality it's not so”, so be careful using it to praise someone: 「書類の上では優秀ですね」 will be heard as “only excellent on paper”, which is sarcastic and rude.
The reading is easy to get wrong: 「の上では」 is read 「うえ」, while a Sino-Japanese noun plus 「上」 is read 「じょう」 (「法律上」, 「形式上」). ✕「ほうりつうえ」.
When a verb comes before it, it is usually another pattern: 「確認した上で」 (“after...”) and 「生活する上で」 (“in the course of...”). 「の上では」 follows a noun.
「机の上では」 (“on the desk”) is a literal position and not this pattern.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with a friend in early spring.
daily.example: By the calendar it's spring, yet it's snowing.

daily.title: On the news
daily.description: The news explains economic data.
daily.example: Statistically the unemployment rate is falling, but it doesn't feel that way.

work.title: Checking a contract
work.description: A legal staff member reports to their boss.
work.example: Under the contract, our company bears no responsibility.

work.title: Analyzing financial statements
work.description: An accountant explains the situation to management.
work.example: On the books we're in the black, but our cash flow is tight.

etymology: 「上(うえ)」 originally means “top” or “above”, and extended to “on a certain level or aspect”. The 「は」 in 「の上では」 is contrastive and often hints at a gap with reality.

similar.title: 〜上（じょう）
similar.explanation: Same origin and close in meaning. Adding 「上（じょう）」 straight to a Sino-Japanese noun (「法律上」, 「形式上」) is more concise and literary. 「の上では」 also takes native Japanese nouns (「暦の上では」, 「数字の上では」) and sounds a little softer.

similar.title: 〜からいうと・〜からいえば
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「からいうと」 means judging from some standpoint or angle (「品質からいうと、こちらが上だ」) and is often used to reach a conclusion. 「の上では」 focuses on “this is so on a certain level” and often hints at a gap with reality.

similar.title: 〜点で・〜という点では
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both limit the angle of evaluation. 「点で」 stresses “in this respect” and is often used to compare strengths and weaknesses (「値段の点では満足だ」). 「の上では」 mostly follows data, documents or rules and stresses “on the surface, nominally”.

similar.title: 〜上で
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜上で」 follows a verb and means “after...” (「確認した上で」) or “in the course of...” (「生活する上で」). It looks like 「の上では」 after a noun, but what comes before and the meaning differ.

formation: 「上（うえ）」 originally means “the top of something”, extended to “a level or aspect”. 「Noun + の上」 means “on the level the noun represents”, 「で」 limits the scope, and 「は」 sets that scope in contrast. Because of the contrastive 「は」, the implication is “so on this level, but not necessarily in other aspects (reality)”, so the pairing of nominal and actual, as in 「暦の上では春だが、まだ寒い」, is the typical use. Attaching Sino-Japanese nouns directly to 「上（じょう）」 follows the same idea in a Sino-Japanese style.

title: 〜ぬ (negative)
meaning: A classical negative auxiliary that equals 「ない」. Today it appears mostly in set phrases, writing, and before nouns.
connection: Verb nai-form stem + ぬ (する→せぬ, 来る→こぬ)

senses.label: Before a noun
senses.meaning: Placed before a noun as a modifier, like 「〜ない + noun」. Many are fixed phrases: 「見知らぬ人」, 「思わぬ事故」, 「予期せぬ出来事」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form stem + ぬ + noun
examples: A stranger asked me for directions.
I ran into a friend somewhere I didn't expect.
Something unexpected happened.

senses.label: Set phrases
senses.meaning: Preserved in proverbs and idioms, such as 「知らぬ間に」 (before you know it), 「言わぬが花」 (some things are better left unsaid), and 「知らぬが仏」 (ignorance is bliss).
senses.connection: Fixed expressions
examples: I fell asleep before I knew it.
Some things are better left unsaid.

senses.label: Sentence-final negative
senses.meaning: Used at the end of a sentence or to link clauses. It sounds old-fashioned, stiff, or emphatic, and appears in novels, speeches, and period dramas.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form stem + ぬ(。)／ぬよう
examples: Such behavior can never be forgiven.
Please be very careful so that no accidents occur.

notes: The negative of 「する」 is 「せぬ」, not 「しぬ」 (which would read as 「死ぬ」, “to die”). For 「来る」 it is 「こぬ」.

Don't confuse it with the classical 「ぬ」 of completion. The completive 「ぬ」 attaches to the continuative form: 「秋来ぬ」 is read 「あききぬ」, “autumn has come”. The negative 「ぬ」 attaches to the imperfective form: 「来ぬ」 is read 「こぬ」, “doesn't come”. The same spelling has the opposite reading and meaning.
「ぬ」 is used to modify a noun or end a sentence; to connect to a following action, use 「ず」: ✕「知らぬに」 → ○「知らずに」. 「知らぬ間に」 is fine because 「ぬ」 modifies the noun 「間」.
Ending a sentence with 「〜ぬ」 in everyday talk sounds old-fashioned, like a period drama. The colloquial 「〜ん」 (「知らん」, 「わからん」) is very casual and rude to superiors or clients; say 「存じません」 or 「わかりません」.

daily.title: Telling about a surprise
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about something unexpected on a trip.
daily.example: I got caught up in unexpected trouble while traveling.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a mysterious visitor.
daily.example: One night, a strange man came to visit.

daily.title: Watching a period drama
daily.description: A samurai's line in a period drama.
daily.example: I shall never forget this kindness.

work.title: Safety notice
work.description: Safety instructions posted in a factory.
work.example: To prevent accidents, always do an inspection before starting work.

work.title: On the news
work.description: A news report on a sudden incident.
work.example: Faced with an unexpected situation, those involved are scrambling to respond.

etymology: 「ぬ」 is the attributive form of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」. In modern Japanese 「ない」 replaced it, but it survives in idioms, written language, and forms like 「ん」 (as in 「知らん」).

similar.title: 〜ない (verb negative form)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「ない」 is the standard modern negative and works anywhere. 「ぬ」 means the same, but survives only in set expressions (「見知らぬ」, 「思わぬ」) and in literary or archaic style.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「ず」 and 「ぬ」 are different conjugated forms of the same classical negative auxiliary: 「ぬ」 modifies nouns, while 「ず」 connects: 「朝ご飯を食べずに出かけた」 (“left without eating breakfast”).

similar.title: 〜ねばならない
similar.explanation: Same origin. The 「ね」 in 「ねばならない」 is also a conjugated form of this negative auxiliary (the realis form); 「ねば」 = “if not...”, and the whole means “must...”, in written style.

formation: 「ぬ」 is the attributive form of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」. It attaches to the imperfective stem of a verb (the form with 「ない」 removed from the nai-form), as in 「知ら＋ぬ」. The attributive form is used to modify nouns, so expressions like 「見知らぬ人」 and 「思わぬ事故」, “ぬ + noun”, are the most stable survivors. Later the attributive form also came to end sentences, so 「許せぬ」 can appear at the end of a sentence, but it feels archaic and stiff. It is generally thought that in speech 「ぬ」 shifted further to 「ん」, giving 「知らん」 and the 「ん」 at the end of 「〜ません」.

meaning: A honorific request used to politely ask someone to do something: “we kindly ask you to ...”, “please ...”.
connection: お + native verb masu-stem + 願う／ご + Sino-Japanese verb stem + 願う

senses.label: We kindly ask ...
senses.meaning: Politely asks the listener to do something: “please ...”, “we ask that you ...”. More formal and polite than 「お〜ください」. Common in announcements, notices, and business.
senses.connection: お待ち／ご遠慮／ご理解／ご注意 + 願います
examples: Please wait a moment.
Authorized personnel only.
Please watch your step.

senses.label: Could you please ...?
senses.meaning: The potential forms 「お〜願えますか」 and 「お〜願えませんか」 make a softer request: “could you please ...?”.
senses.connection: お／ご + verb stem + 願えますか／願えませんか
examples: Could you come by again tomorrow?
Could you fill this in here, please?

senses.label: I would like you to ...
senses.meaning: 「お〜願いたい」 shows what the speaker wants the other person to do. It's polite but can sound quite firm. 「お引き取り願いたい」 means “I must ask you to leave”.
senses.connection: お／ご + verb stem + 願いたい
examples: I must ask you to leave for today.
I would ask you to keep this matter strictly confidential.

notes: 「お引き取り願います／願いたい」 literally means “please take your leave”, but in practice it is an order to get out, “please leave, we won't serve you”, and is very forceful. To see a guest off normally, say 「お気をつけてお帰りください」; misuse gravely offends the guest.
「ご遠慮願います」 is a polite prohibition, “please refrain from...”: 「店内での撮影はご遠慮願います」 = photography is not allowed in the shop, not “please be modest”.
Native Japanese verbs take 「お」 and Sino-Japanese verbs take 「ご」: ✕「お確認願います」 → ○「ご確認願います」; ✕「ご待ち願います」 → ○「お待ち願います」.

「お〜願います」 is businesslike and a one-sided demand, suited to announcements and notices. When asking a client or superior for help face to face, 「お〜いただけますか」 or 「お〜いただけないでしょうか」 is softer and more fitting.

daily.title: Theater announcement
daily.description: An announcement before the show starts.
daily.example: Please remain quiet during the performance.

daily.title: Station announcement
daily.description: A warning as a train arrives.
daily.example: For your safety, please step back behind the white line.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Asking a client to check an attachment.
work.example: Please review the attached documents.

work.title: Turning away an unwanted visitor
work.description: Politely refusing a salesperson who came without an appointment.
work.example: I'm very sorry, but I must ask you to leave for today.

work.title: Asking for cooperation in a meeting
work.description: The chair asks attendees to turn off their phones.
work.example: Please turn off your mobile phones.

etymology: Made from the honorific prefix 「お／ご」, the verb's masu-stem, and the verb 「願う」 (to ask, to request). It belongs to the same 「お + stem + verb」 honorific family as 「お〜する」 and 「お〜ください」.

similar.title: お〜ください
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「お〜ください」 is a direct request and the most common when serving guests (「お待ちください」). 「お〜願います」 is more formal and businesslike, mostly for announcements, notices and requests to an unspecified audience.

similar.title: 〜お〜いただく・ご〜いただく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「お〜いただく」 speaks from the viewpoint of “receiving” the other person's action, humble and soft (「お越しいただきありがとうございます」). 「お〜願う」 speaks from the viewpoint of “requesting”, and is more one-sided.

similar.title: 〜をお願いします
similar.explanation: Same origin (both use 「願う」). 「〜をお願いします」 is a noun + 「を」 + 「お願い」 and takes any noun (「コーヒーをお願いします」). 「お〜願う」 sandwiches a verb between 「お」 and 「願う」 and is used only to request an action from the other person.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜ていただけませんか」 is colloquial and indirect, suited to face-to-face requests. 「お〜願えませんか」 means the same, but is more formal and literary, common on the phone and in business.

formation: It is formed from the honorific prefix 「お／ご」 + the continuative form of a verb + the verb 「願う」. The continuative form can act as a noun, and with 「お／ご」 it becomes an honorific for the other person's action (「お待ち」, 「ご確認」); adding 「願う」 (“humbly request”) gives “I request that you do...”. This is the same “お + continuative + verb” construction as 「お〜する」 and 「お〜ください」, with a request verb at the end. Since the core is the speaker's one-sided request, the tone is formal but a bit businesslike: turn it into the potential 「願えますか」 and it becomes a question, softer; turn it into the desiderative 「願いたい」 and it sounds firm.

meaning: Something is done very poorly or hardly at all, with a tone of dissatisfaction or criticism: “not properly”, “barely”.
connection: ろくに + verb negative form; ろくな + noun + ない

senses.label: Not properly / barely
senses.meaning: Something is done far too little, almost not at all: “not properly”, “hardly”. Often shows the speaker's dissatisfaction, criticism, or self-mockery.
senses.connection: ろくに + verb nai-form／ず／ません
examples: I've been so busy I've barely slept.
He took the exam with hardly any studying.
Please don't object without even listening properly.

senses.label: No decent ...
senses.meaning: 「ろくな + noun + ない」 means there's nothing decent or satisfying: “not a single decent ...”.
senses.connection: ろくな + noun + が／も + ない
examples: There's nothing decent in the fridge.
There hasn't been any good news lately.

senses.label: Good-for-nothing
senses.meaning: 「ろくでもない」 means worthless or terrible: “useless”, “rotten”.
senses.connection: ろくでもない + noun
examples: You're thinking up some stupid idea again, aren't you?

notes: It must be matched with a negative: ✕「ろくに寝た」 → ○「ろくに寝ていない」. Without the negative it doesn't work.
It carries strong dissatisfaction and disparagement. To a superior or client, 「ろくに説明もしないで」 is seriously rude; in formal settings, or about yourself, 「十分に〜ていない」 or 「あまり〜ていない」 is safer.
「ろくでもない」 means “worthless, awful”; calling a person 「ろくでもない男」 is a harsh insult that shouldn't be used lightly about others.
「ろくに」 modifies verbs and 「ろくな」 modifies nouns: ✕「ろくに物がない」 → ○「ろくな物がない」.

daily.title: Complaining about being busy
daily.description: Complaining to a friend before an exam.
daily.example: I was studying for a test and could barely sleep last night.

daily.title: A parent scolding a child
daily.description: A parent is unhappy that the child is a picky eater.
daily.example: You hardly eat your meals and just snack all the time.

daily.title: Grumbling about life
daily.description: Joking about yourself while living alone.
daily.example: It's right before payday, so I haven't eaten anything decent.

work.title: Criticizing work attitude
work.description: A boss is unhappy with a subordinate who cuts corners.
work.example: It's a problem when you come to meetings without even reading the materials properly.

etymology: 「ろく」 is written 「陸」 or 「碌」 and originally meant “flat, proper”, which extended to “decent, satisfactory”. Paired with a negative, it means “not decent, not enough”.

similar.title: ちっとも〜ない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both pair with a negative. 「ちっとも〜ない」 is the complete negation “not at all” (「ちっとも分からない」). 「ろくに〜ない」 means “didn't do it properly”: something was done, but far from enough, with a critical tone.

similar.title: 〜もしないで
similar.explanation: Close in meaning, often combined as 「ろくに〜もしないで」. 「〜もしないで」 stresses “didn't even do what should be done” (「調べもしないで」). 「ろくに」 stresses “didn't do it adequately”. Together, the reproach is stronger.

similar.title: めったに〜ない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (both can be “hardly ever”). 「めったに〜ない」 describes low frequency, something rarely happening (「めったに休まない」), with no judgment. 「ろくに〜ない」 describes doing it poorly, with dissatisfaction.

formation: 「ろく」 is generally thought to come from 「陸（ろく）」, originally “flat, proper”, extended to “decent, satisfactory”; the kanji 「碌」 is a borrowed spelling. Adding the adverbial ending 「に」 makes 「ろくに」, “decently, adequately”, and adding 「な」 makes 「ろくな」, “decent”. They pair only with a negative, “didn't do it properly” or “there's nothing decent”, giving “didn't ... properly” or “there isn't a single decent...”, with the speaker's dissatisfaction. 「ろくでもない」 is 「ろくで」 + 「も」 + 「ない」, “not even decent”, extended to “utterly awful”.
